problem:
A quadratic equation with real coefficients has a complex root $x=2+5\text{i}.$ Given that the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ in the equation is $1,$ find the equation. Write your answer in the form $a{x}^{2}+bx+c=0,$ where $a,$ $b,$ and $c$ are real constants.

{{field-1}}$=0$
worked_solution:
Since the quadratic equation has real coefficients and $x=2+5\text{i}$ is a root, we know that its complex conjugate $x=2-5\text{i}$ is also a root. Therefore, using the zero product property, we can write a quadratic equation with the required roots as follows:

$$
(x-(2+5\text{i}))(x-(2-5\text{i}))=0
$$

By expanding the parentheses, we can write the equation in standard form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-x(2+5\text{i})-x(2-5\text{i})+(2+5\text{i})(2-5\text{i}) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-2x-\cancel{5x\text{i}}-2x+\cancel{5x\text{i}}+4-25{\text{i}}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-4x+4+25 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-4x+29 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

When the parabola intersects the $x$-axis, we must have $y=0.$ So, we set $y=0$ and solve the resulting equation for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & =4(0+\frac{1}{2}) \\ {x}^{2} & =2 \\ x & =\pm \sqrt{2}\text{ }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the intersection points, from left to right, are $(-\sqrt{2},0)$ and $(\sqrt{2},0).$

To find the slope at a point, we use implicit differentiation to calculate the derivative of the curve, assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{1/2}-{y}^{1/2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\ \frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2}-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}) & =0 \\ -\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}) & =-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2} \\ -\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}) & =-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\sqrt{y}}{\sqrt{x}}\end{aligned}
$$

The slope of the tangent at the point $(9,\,4)$ is then given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{(9,\,4)} \\  & ={(\frac{\sqrt{y}}{\sqrt{x}})|}_{(9,\,4)} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{4}}{\sqrt{9}} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we rearrange the equation and isolate $\operatorname{cot}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3-4\operatorname{cot}⁡x & =-2\operatorname{cot}⁡x \\ -2\operatorname{cot}⁡x & =-3 \\ \operatorname{cot}⁡x & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that $\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}.$ Therefore, the given equation is equivalent to

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{2}{3}.
$$

Now, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\text{arctan}(\frac{2}{3})=(33.690\,0…)^{∘}≈{33.690}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${33.690}^{∘}$ lies inside the given domain, our first solution is ${x}_{1}={33.690}^{∘}.$

To generate more solutions, we add and subtract integer multiples of ${180}^{∘}.$ Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2}=-{180}^{∘}+{33.690}^{∘}=-{146.310}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions are $x=-{146.310}^{∘},\,{33.690}^{∘}.$

A circle of radius $k$ centered at the origin has the polar equation $r=k.$

We can compute the radius $k$ of our circle using the Pythagorean theorem, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}k & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{6}^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{36+4} \\  & =\sqrt{40} \\  & =2\sqrt{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the circle is $r=2\sqrt{10}.$
